items.summary: Arbitration in India cannot deliver on its promise of speed if hearings are being fixed three, four or five months apart, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said on Thursday, while calling for arbitrators’ calendars to be checked before they are appointed. He said the purpose of arbitration was speed in dispute resolution, but crowded schedules of arbitrators were contributing to long gaps between hearings. He said he was impressed by an institutional model where an arbitrator’s calendar is sought before appointment. “ What happens is, in the absence of such a system in India, arbitrators are so busy that today there is an arbitration hearing; the next day to get this hearing will be after a few months, 3, 4, 5 months. That's the problem ,” Mehta said. SG Mehta was speaking during a fireside chat with Nish Shetty, Partner at Clifford Chance and Co-Chair of the Mumbai Centre for International Arbitration (MCIA) , on what India needs to do to make its arbitration system more effective and attractive to parties. The chat was organised as a part of India ADR Week 2026. Shetty asked what India needed to do to encourage parties from within and outside the country to have confidence that arbitrations in India would be conducted in a familiar and dependable manner. "I was really impressed by one model - one of the institutional models where, before appointing an arbitrator, his calendar is asked for," SG said. "There is a request for the calendar. And if the institution feels that his calendar permits conclusion of the arbitration within the statutorily fixed time, then only is he appointed." SG Mehta said India should consider adopting a similar mechanism. “ So we should incorporate institutional arbitration with a similar calendar appraisal system .” SG Mehta also backed a greater shift towards institutional arbitration over ad hoc arbitration. “If we concentrate more on institutional arbitration than individual arbitration, meaning that where the institution would choose the arbitrators and not the parties, then that might be a real boost in the arbitration.” The discussion also touched upon the relatively small share of institutional arbitration in India. Shetty pointed out that MCIA had crossed 200 matters in its first decade, while an estimated 50,000 ad hoc arbitrations were taking place in India at any given point. items.title: Maharashtra anti-conversion law challenged before Bombay High Court
items.summary: AA petition has been filed before the principal bench of the Bombay High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026 . [Maulana Halimullah Farooque Ahemed Khan v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.] The petition has been filed by 70-year-old Islamic scholar Maulana Halimullah Farooque Ahemed Khan. According to the plea, the newly enacted law infringes fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution. As per the plea, while prohibiting forced or fraudulent marriages is valid, such power cannot extend to state surveillance of consensual inter-faith relationships or voluntary religious conversions. “The choice of a life partner and the decision concerning one's faith constitute facets of personal autonomy, dignity, privacy and decisional freedom protected under Articles 21 and 25 of the Constitution,” the plea reads. Section 9(2) prescribes enhanced punishment for converting women. The plea terms this gender-discriminatory. The plea has also assailed Section 2(a) for defining "allurement" in vague, over broad terms. Phrases like "better lifestyle" and "divine healing" used in the provision would bar legitimate religious discourse and charity. As per the petition, “The threat of criminal proceedings, arrest, non-bailable prosecution, mandatory disclosure of personal information and public scrutiny under the impugned Act is capable of deterring individuals, religious organisations and institutions from undertaking legitimate religious teaching, preaching, charitable, humanitarian and related activities.” The plea has also challenged the mandatory 60-day notice before converting from one religion to another. The petition argues that this exposes personal faith choices to public scrutiny and state inquiry, violating privacy. “Where a person voluntarily chooses to change his or her religion, the constitutional inquiry must be confined to whether such decision was made freely, voluntarily and with full and informed consent; the State cannot legitimately investigate the individual’s beliefs, motivations or reasons for such choice merely because the person may have been exposed to religious instruction, persuasion or lawful charitable and humanitarian activities,” the petition states. items.title: Mumbai court grants bail to TISS student arrested for slogans supporting Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam
items.summary: A Mumbai court has granted bail to Abhirup Ashim Paul, a student of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS), who was arrested for allegedly raising slogans supporting jailed activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam. [Abhirup Paul v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.] Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate Dattatray Shankarrao Khedekar observed that Paul had already undergone custodial interrogation for sufficient period. Pertinently, the Court also said that there was no evidence linking him to any Maoist or any other banned organisation. “Prima facie except suspicion, there is no material to link the activities of the accused with mind set of maoist or against the nation or associating with banned organization against India,” the judge noted. The Court observed that having soft copies of the Maoist books and raising campus slogans in support of jailed activists did not amount to anti-national activity and an inference of being a Moaist cannot be drawn from the same. "Merely because of finding of pdf books (on Maoism), the inference of connection with the mind set of maoist can not be draw," the Court ruled. He determined that keeping Paul, a young offender, behind bars on mere suspicion would be unjust and detrimental to his career. The case stemmed from a first information report (FIR) filed on a complaint by the TISS Registrar over an unauthorised campus event. On October 12, 2025, students gathered at the institute to commemorate the death anniversary of the late professor GN Saibaba. During the gathering, the prosecution alleged that students raised slogans demanding the release of Khalid and Imam who are in jail in a case under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). After the sessions court rejected his anticipatory bail plea, Paul was arrested and taken into custody on August 7. The police alleged that Paul’s actions may be linked to a broader threat against the nation and were intended to create hatred in the community. items.summary: The Delhi High Court on Thursday declined to grant wrestler Vinesh Phogat interim relief to participate in the selection trials for the 2026 Senior World Wrestling Championships starting on September 14. items.title: Former Andhra Minister Jogi Ramesh’s daughter-in-law alleges dowry harassment
items.summary: Jogi Meghana, daughter-in-law of former Andhra Pradesh Minister and YSRCP leader Jogi Ramesh, has sought police protection for herself and her parents, alleging dowry harassment, domestic violence and attempts on her life by her husband and in-laws. Meghana met Andhra Pradesh Governor S Abdul Nazeer at Raj Bhavan on Wednesday, September 9 and submitted a representation seeking protection and a fair, time-bound investigation into the case registered on the basis of her complaint. In her representation, Meghana alleged that her parents had spent around Rs 5 crore on her wedding and gave gold and silver articles, cash and other gifts. She claimed that her in-laws later demanded another Rs 5 crore, a Toyota Fortuner and diamond jewellery. She has accused her husband Rajeev, father-in-law Jogi Ramesh, mother-in-law Shakuntala and other relatives of subjecting her to physical and mental harassment over the alleged dowry demands. Meghana has also alleged that there were several attempts to harm her. She alleged that Rajeev tried to push her into the water from a boat during a trip to Goa despite knowing that she could not swim. She also alleged an incident at a farmhouse in Ghatkesar, Telangana, and claimed that she was assaulted at her matrimonial home in April 2026. According to her allegations, she was strangled and smothered during the incident. “My parents and I are facing life threats from my in-laws Jogi Ramesh, Shakuntala, my husband Rajeev, and other family members. Please protect us and take immediate action against those who directly and indirectly harassed me,” Meghana said in her representation. The Ibrahimpatnam police registered a case on July 24 against Ramesh, Rajeev and nine other family members based on Meghana’s complaint. The case includes allegations under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the Dowry Prohibition Act, including cruelty, dowry harassment and attempt to murder. Meghana has also alleged that her in-laws concealed information about their religious practices before her marriage. She said she was told that the family followed Hindu traditions but later discovered that they practised Christianity. She clarified that she had no objection to their religion, but alleged that the information was not disclosed to her before the marriage. The dispute subsequently became a political issue. items.title: Fishermen, political parties oppose TN’s proposed Secretariat complex at Foreshore
items.summary: The Tamil Nadu government’s in-principle approval for a new Secretariat and Legislative Assembly complex at Foreshore Estate in Chennai has drawn opposition over its proposed coastal location. The Rs 1,200-crore project will come up on 25.55 acres in Mylapore town, with most of the land belonging to the Tamil Nadu Housing Board. The site is at Pattinapakkam, close to Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay’s residence. The government order issued on September 8 said three committees have been formed to expedite the project. One will select an architectural consultant, while the other two will finalise the preliminary and final building designs. The Public Works Department has been asked to submit a detailed project report and estimates within three months. Vijay had announced the proposal in the Assembly on September 3, saying that the new 20 lakh sq foot complex would house the Legislative Assembly, offices of the Chief Minister and Ministers, and various government departments. It is proposed to have modern facilities including parking, conference halls, public service centres, and fire-safety and accessibility infrastructure. The government has cited space constraints at Fort St George, where the Secretariat and Assembly currently function. Vijay said only about four acres of the 107-acre campus is under the state government’s control, with the rest under the Defence Ministry and the Archaeological Survey of India. The choice of Pattinapakkam, however, has prompted objections from political leaders and fishing communities. PMK president Anbumani Ramadoss has urged the government to abandon the proposal and instead establish an integrated administrative city on 500 to 1,000 acres outside Chennai. He said the area already faces severe traffic pressure, with Santhome Church, schools and other high-footfall institutions nearby. Anbumani also questioned whether the proposed site would be large enough to accommodate the complex along with mandatory green spaces, parking, emergency facilities and public transport infrastructure. He argued that a larger administrative township would better serve the state’s needs over the next 100 years. DMK Rajya Sabha MP P Wilson questioned the project’s impact on fishermen and existing infrastructure. items.title: Gold rings or rights? The patriarchal underpinnings of Tamil Nadu’s Thaimaman scheme
items.summary: The Tamil Nadu government’s recent announcement of the Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram (TTM) (literally translates to Maternal Uncle’s Gold Ring scheme) – a one-gram gold ring to be given to babies born in government hospitals – needs to be evaluated through a gender lens. The scheme also raises the question of what the role of the state in welfare is and what its desirable role should be. The nomenclature and the narrative around the TTM scheme in particular reinforce the image of a patriarchal state that sees itself as protecting and caring for its citizens through its largesse, rather than one that represents people and pledges to carry forward the rights enshrined in the Constitution. Tamil Nadu is known for its welfare programmes – many of them progressive – setting up strong state institutions that are a model for the rest of the country. It has been a pioneering state in providing entitlements such as school mid-day meals, which over time have expanded to include breakfast, cover children up to class 10, and serve eggs on all days of the week. The state has led in many other ways – through reforms in the health sector ensuring a more democratised workforce, lower out-of-pocket expenditure in the public sector, and a reasonably well functioning primary healthcare system. Community kitchens, universal Public Distribution System (PDS), strengthened anganwadi centres, better paid frontline workers have all been the trademarks of the welfare state in Tamil Nadu. The state has also been a frontrunner in providing maternity entitlements. The Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy Maternity Benefit Scheme, in place since 1987, was amended in 2006 to raise the cash assistance to Rs 6,000, years before the country’s first Union maternity scheme, the Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojana, was launched in 2010 at just Rs 4,000 (raised to Rs 6,000 only in 2013, to meet the National Food Security Act’s mandated minimum). The Tamil Nadu scheme has always been explicitly framed as compensating pregnant women for wage loss. Over time, the benefit was enhanced to Rs 18,000 (Rs 14,000 in cash and nutrition kits worth Rs 4,000), while the current national scheme, the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana, gives only Rs 5,000.
